commits.message:
Apply Shellbox machine controls and preserve sandbox cleanup (#9641)

Apply machine resource settings and per-command execution users across
the Shellbox backends. Reject unsupported overrides and nonpositive CPU
or storage requests. Preserve Docker image working directories,
directory contents during transfer, and cleanup after cancellation
during container creation.

Create Daytona sandboxes from reusable snapshots. Give each machine its
own SDK client so worker threads do not share event-loop state. Close
clients on failure and machine cleanup, preserve uploaded file
permissions, and apply startup deadlines and network policies.
Dockerfiles with `ADD` require a prebuilt registry image because the
pinned SDK does not upload those inputs.

Snapshot polling uses exponential backoff within the startup deadline.
The local suite passed 20 tests with the Daytona SDK installed,
including pending-snapshot timeouts and client cleanup. Two Harbor
adapter tests were skipped because Harbor is absent from that
environment.

Builds on [the merged image-cache
fix](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9640). [The rollout
engine](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9623) depends on
these machine operations.

Part of #9612

Reuse Shellbox image builds across equivalent local contexts (#9640)

Reuse prepared images when identical Docker build contexts occupy
different local directories. Compute the cache key from relative paths
and build inputs. Content changes still trigger a new build. Cache hits
retain the current caller’s source so QEMU staging can read its
Dockerfile after the original directory is deleted.

copy, QEMU bundle staging, and a changed payload.

This is a prerequisite for the Shellbox machine changes and [the rollout
engine](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9623).

commits.author: atqamar
commits.message:
[CatCountCanary] Launch pretrained Qwen with Megatron

The CatCount GPU canary trains a pretrained Qwen model with Megatron and checks sampled reward on counting prompts.

The CLI defaults to the one-step dry preset, with evaluation before training and after that step and no score stopping threshold. The asynchronous gate preset uses seed 17, behavior clipping, staleness 2 and learning rate 2e-6 on four H100s across two hosts. Its sampled evaluation runs before training and every five steps, stopping at a score of at least 0.65 with a 30-step cap. Greedy, held-out and extrapolation evaluations are reported. Checkpoints and Hugging Face export require explicit flags. Export also enables its prerequisite checkpoint, and the launcher persists terminal results at a per-user run directory.

The launcher reads the immutable Qwen snapshot from the rl-canaries S3 prefix and writes run outputs under its GPU runs prefix. Commands include a 4-CPU, 16-GB-memory, 8-GB-disk coordinator and a 20-minute deadline. Each optimizer step reports training-rank weight checksum consistency.

The final main-pin async run passed the complete spec and stopped at step 10. Sampled evaluation reward on training prompts went from 0.2454 to 0.6845. Both GPU tasks took 8 minutes 31 seconds; the coordinator took 10 minutes 36 seconds, with zero preemptions. The README records its Marin and MarinSkyRL revisions and [measured rewards](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-cat-count-canary/runs/1jr0tjpg).

Historical reward replay passes healthy runs and rejects sign reversal, corrupted rollout probabilities and unstable learning rates. The completed-step divergence control finishes training and fails only on checksum mismatches. This validation covers the asynchronous canary with checkpoints and export off; synchronous CI, checkpoint/export behavior and tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism are outside its coverage.

[Design document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1N4JDNHVRS9hveJ-wC2UfqnrgVPDbj4ZcGac3FShS7XM/).

[shellbox] Support remote ShellSim download targets (#9550)

Allow ShellSim trial logs to download into Harbor remote targets.
ShellSim writes only to local paths; remote file and directory downloads
stage locally and upload through `rigging.StoragePath` in a worker
thread. Local targets use the direct path. This avoids the
`Path(S3Path)` error that masked the original trial failure.

Use `StoragePath` for Marin's Harbor job and AIME log paths. Harbor's
`JobConfig` validates `jobs_dir` into the runtime path type it requires.
Declare `marin-rigging` in the ShellSim extra and the isolated Harbor
environment.

Fixes #9547

commits.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
commits.message:
[zephyr] Preserve path-only file projections (#9560)

Selecting only the injected file path now returns that field for each
row that passes range and filter selection. The previous empty
projection became a request for every source column, adding those fields
to output and reading unnecessary Parquet data.

Vortex rejects empty projections, so its reader carries one source
column through range and filter evaluation, then drops it. The affected
safe suite passed: 1,788 tests, 3 skipped, and 6 expected failures.

Co-authored-by: loom <claude-max-1@openathena.ai>

commits.author: atqamar
commits.message:
[rl-mismatch] Finestore: store probe inputs, scores, and provenance

Store frozen RL responses, scorer log probabilities and run provenance as three typed tables. Log-probability vectors use float32 Arrow lists. Expert-route arrays carry shape, dtype and a validity mask beside their raw bytes. Scorer, update, trainer mode and prefix-cache mode identify each score row. The manifest records archive completion, tokenizer identity, starting weights and both relative probe updates and absolute trainer steps.

Keep this contract in `finestore.mismatch_probe`, next to `finestore.eval`, so MarinSkyRL can write it without depending on `marin-core` and Marin can read it without importing trainer or inference packages. The FineStore archive round-trip retains token IDs, compact routes, distinct updates and modes, float32 scores and completed provenance. Projected-scan test coverage is removed from this PR; FineStore's core tests own scan projection.

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[grug] Train Snowball on synthetic tokens through the trainer (#9613)

Issue #9462 asks for a Snowball training baseline on one 8-GPU AMD node:
step time, tokens/s, MFU, peak memory, and the top ops from a profile,
which picks the first AMD kernel to write. No existing entry point
trains Snowball on synthetic data: the pipeline experiment depends on
NVIDIA's JaxPP, and the hero experiment's synthetic mode uses a
different expert layout. This harness, in experiments/grug beside the
other synthetic-data Grug trainers, is the reproducible path for that
baseline, so it can be rerun after each kernel change. Unlike its
neighbours it carries no model copy: it drives Levanter's SnowballConfig
directly, because the point is to measure the production code path.

The script trains Snowball on uniform-random tokens through Levanter's
Trainer for a fixed number of steps, with Adam, mixed precision, and the
model's per-layer rematerialization, and logs step time, tokens/s, MFU,
and peak device memory. Presets cover a tiny shape for CPU checks, a
4-layer shape at full width, and the full 26-layer 67B model. It can
profile a window of steps, and it runs on AMD GPUs with reference
attention and XLA ragged_dot. No checkpoint is written: the forced final
save of the 67B model and Adam state would be about 1 TB.

MFU uses a FLOPs-per-token estimate computed in the script, so
snowball.py, which pins one checkpoint architecture, is unchanged. The
estimate charges full-context attention on every 4th layer through the
existing global_every path of lm_flops_per_token. Snowball's final layer
is also a long layer, which the stride misses: a 0.4% undercount at a
4096-token context for the 26-layer model.

Examples go straight to the loader. LmDataConfig's mixer wraps a dataset
shorter than its 2048-example block, so a small synthetic set repeated
about a third of its examples and the 67B model memorized them, pulling
the loss below ln(vocab). With no repeats the loss is a leak check: it
cannot fall below ln(vocab).

A global batch of 1 is rejected with an explanatory error. Under an
explicit mesh, JAX 0.11 drops the sharding of the (1, 1) slice that
jnp.roll takes from the (1, seq_len) token grid in the next-token loss
and then refuses to concatenate it with the sharded remainder. Single
device runs need --batch-size 2.

Part of #9462

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[finelog] Match top-level columns when reading bounds (#9619)

Read Parquet bounds using the full top-level column path. A list element
named `item` can precede a scalar column with the same name; selecting
statistics by leaf name could use the list's bounds to exclude matching
scalar rows during query planning. Apply the same path matching to
catalog key bounds.

Follow up on #9618.

Co-authored-by: github-actions[bot] <41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com>

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[finelog] Prune ranges before loading substring indexes (#9618)

Exclude cached Parquet segments whose signed integer min/max statistics
cannot match the query before loading substring indexes. Keep the
computed trigram row-selection masks for the rest of the query, so cache
eviction between planning stages does not require loading the same
indexes again. Missing local Parquet files or incomplete statistics
leave segments available for the normal scan.

Increase the Marin hub's decoded index cache from 1 GiB to 3 GiB. The
hub's retained log index bundles occupy 1.38 GiB on disk, before
decoding overhead and indexes from other namespaces.

With 32 hard-linked copies of a production log shard, a DEBUG search
after the shard's latest timestamp planned in 29 ms initially and 10 ms
on repetition, down from 22.8 s and 22.4 s. The local debug build used a
16 MiB decoded index cache; file bytes were already cached by the
operating system. These measurements isolate planning behavior and do
not predict production latency.

commits.author: Helw150
commits.message:
Gate verified evaluation cohorts before launch and comparison (#9461)

Add `-verified` launch scripts for the September 16 and September 24
evaluation policies. Each selected benchmark gets a separate H100 serve
group sized by the model YAML, and a cohort may contain any subset of
its benchmarks. Before submission, the launcher checks benchmark
settings, model configuration, source YAML digests, and evaluator
commits against the chosen policy. EvalDash excludes records that
violate a verified policy from scored views and shows their rejection
reasons.

The dashboard defaults to the September 24 verified cohort. Historical
named cohorts and `all` remain selectable; `all` chooses the newest
eligible run per benchmark across cohorts. An asterisk marks
historical-cohort and `all` panel and comparison views because their
runs have not been checked for comparable settings. Model configurations
with different source YAMLs get separate comparison identities even if
they share a model name. September 24 chat benchmarks require explicit
`enable_thinking` true or false; September 16 keeps each model's saved
setting.

Verified launches execute the cohort's Evalchemy commit and use its
frozen Harbor lock for both preflight and workers. Harbor run provenance
includes the dependency versions in that lock. The pinned Evalchemy
revision includes [the fix for sending multiple chat-template flags
together](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/183).

Hosted Pi launches require an explicit model- or policy-level thinking
format, validated during preflight before submission. Grug uses
`chat-template` and Qwen uses `qwen-chat-template`; these settings do
not change reasoning modes.

Model detail URLs record the selected cohort. Links from the panel,
comparison, and run pages preserve the cohort they display; unqualified
model links resolve to the dashboard default. Evalchemy code-task
coverage uses `scored_count` when it matches the attempted item count,
so full HumanEval+/MBPP+ runs do not show zero graded coverage. If
`scored_count` differs from attempted count, coverage remains ungraded.
